title: The Shakespeare jazz album with Dick Hyman
summary: Compared with Cleo Laine's Shakespeare record, Dick Hyman's arrangements were originally made for Earl Wrightson and the album used Rusty Dedrick, Bucky Pizzarelli and Milt Hinton.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Sure. Well that could just be, because on your next album, you took the extraordinary step of going four hundred years to dig up some material.
Like I said, we keep going farther and farther back all the time.

Anyway, I must say, this is one of the three great Shakespeare jazz albums, I supposed. You have mention Duke Ellington and Billy Strayhorn, I guess. He gets credit on it, too. The album, 'Such Sweet Thunder,' which is, from when? The mid-50's I think they did that?
Yeah.

And there's an album that Cleo Laine recorded in England with Johnny Dankworth, which is rather different in conception from yours. And is the album in question that we're going to go on and talk about which is entitled, 'Sullivan, Shakespeare, Hyman,' on the Monmouth-Evergreen label, recorded in June of 1971 These are settings of works of Shakespeare

put to music by Dick Hyman, aren't they? Yes. It seems that, well, years before that when Dick had accompanied -- been part of the group and was accompanying on some of our earlier recordings, especially the ones with just a trio -- he said that it was the first time that he had accompanied a singer. And he had me in mind when he decided to do this album of Shakespeare's lyrics. Of course, this was not my first brush with Shakespeare, because I had recorded "A Lover And His Lass" earlier in my career.
But it was a different setting.

Not only that, but it was a different arrangement altogether. But there have been -- I believed there had been plenty music set to Shakespeare's lyrics, and all of it's different. I imagined in each generation or every once in a while, someone gets the ideas that they must

write some music to some of the Shakespeare sonnets or lyrics, or some of his -- the songs that are listed in his work.
But Dick went to work, and I think this was about a ten or fifteen-year span between the time he wanted to do this and the time that he finally got around to doing it.
Yeah, because some of these had prepared for some television programs, I think.
Yes.
Well the original recording of these tunes was done by Earl Wrightson. And I have an album with Earl Wrightson playing these tunes with the full orchestra, and plus a chorus of singers behind him.
With the same Latin American rhythms you have on --
The same arrangements. It's the very same arrangements, but not swinging. You know, real straight.
Well, without such a genius that Maxine Sullivan represents.

So, Dick wasn't quite as sat -- Well that, I supposed he had to do, because they probably -- he probably was commissioned to do this catalog and put it out. There is a catalog with just the music and the lyrics in there by Dick Hyman. And so he contacted me and told me what he wanted to do. I said, 'Okay, we'll take a chance.' And at the time when he approached me, there was a possibility there might be in the offing an opportunity to do these things on television or whatever as part of a production -- a show, so to speak. So I rehearsed with Dick for about three or four days. And then set up the studio for us to record. And, of course, we recorded these things in three days. On certain numbers, he brought the harpsichord in for accompaniment. And other days he played the piano.

And, of course, he brought Rusty Dedrick in and Rusty played trumpet and flugel frugal horn.
Bucky Pizzarelli on guitar, Milt Hinton on bass and Don Lamond on drums.
The arrangements that he brought in are -- as I said, they were very skeletal -- and the trumpet and fflugel horn that Rusty Dedrick played was more or less just for effect.
I was very impressed with the fact that Dick kept the tunes, in my estimation, in what they sound like they might've sounded in the day that Shakespeare wrote them.
The music has this Elizebethan flavor. And I enjoyed doing them.
But it's not at all heavy handed. I mean, some attempt to sound Elizabethan can be so artificial.
Yeah, right, absolutely.
And coy.
Yeah.
But these -- they're simple but they're the form that they take is a little unusual, which,
